f7e4a768: Why You Keep Turning Off Screen Time
c5fd8ed8: Why do I keep turning off Screen Time?
11bce276: Because you hold the passcode. Screen Time asks you for permission at the exact moment you are least able to refuse, so the limit is enforced by the version of you who wants to break it. The fix is structural: move the decision to another person rather than trying harder.
f1cb13d7: Is there a way to lock Screen Time so I can't change it?
230981b6: Not reliably on your own, because any passcode you set is a passcode you know. The practical options are having someone else set a code you never see, or using an app with a built-in approval flow where another person approves each unlock.
a9e7a04e: Does deleting a social media app work?
4140618c: Only briefly. Reinstalling takes seconds and your account still exists, so deletion raises the cost of relapse without removing the option. It works best combined with a block you cannot lift yourself.
fafa0f74: How it works Lock levels Compare Guides FAQ
7b140ab8: You set the limit while you were thinking clearly. You removed it while you weren't. That is not a discipline problem — it is a design problem, and it has a fix.
127cf158: By Shuaib Khan · 6 min read · Updated August 2026
df9e01e3: Almost everyone who installs a screen time limit has the same story. The first week works. The second week you tap Ignore Limit once, for a good reason. By the third week the limit is still technically switched on, and it is doing nothing at all.
c5ef5dbd: The usual explanation is that you lack discipline. That explanation is wrong, and believing it makes the problem worse, because it sends you looking for more motivation instead of a better setup.
092134a6: The real problem: you are both the lock and the key
93f7af55: Apple's Screen Time is enforced by a four-digit passcode. You choose that passcode. You know that passcode. So at the exact moment the limit fires, the system asks you for permission — and the version of you being asked is not the version who set the rule.
d21a1271: This is the whole mechanism. It is not that the block is weak. It is that the block asks the wrong person.
dffb24e6: The person who sets a limit on Sunday evening and the person who hits that limit on Wednesday night are, functionally, two different people with two different goals.
837b294f: Behavioural researchers call this a commitment device problem. A commitment device only works when your future self genuinely cannot undo the decision your present self made. A passcode you know is not a commitment device. It is a speed bump with a polite request attached.
23563bc4: Why the usual fixes don't hold
3c9662e1: Reinstalling takes about twenty seconds and your account is still there. Deleting raises the price of relapse slightly; it does not remove the option.
be19c910: Grayscale, home screen tidying, notification cleanup
967dcc52: These genuinely help, and they are worth doing. They reduce the number of times you reach for the phone unconsciously. What they do not do is stop you when you have already decided you want in.
805116b2: People try this. It fails for an obvious reason: you still know it. Difficulty is not the same as impossibility, and the moment you actually want in, difficulty is a formality.
13f9d88c: Giving your passcode to a friend
901852f9: This is closer, and it is the right instinct. The problem is practical rather than conceptual. Your friend now has to be physically nearby, awake, and willing to read out a code every time you have a legitimate reason to get in. It collapses within a week, not because the idea is wrong, but because the logistics are unworkable.
35a1f940: The instinct behind handing over the passcode is correct: move the decision to someone who is not currently craving the app. What that instinct needs is a system that makes it practical, so it survives longer than a few days.
59c5ee06: A working version has four properties:
be2b6930: Someone else holds the decision. Not a timer you can end, not a passcode you know.
e8a16eec: Asking is low-friction. A request they can answer in one tap from wherever they are, not a phone call.
0dddd734: Saying no costs them nothing. If refusing feels socially awkward, they will always say yes and the system is decorative.
35750d7a: Access is temporary. Getting in for a genuine reason should not silently disable the rule for good.
3b8c9742: That last one matters more than it sounds. Most people who abandon a blocker do not consciously quit. They unlock once for a real reason, never re-enable it, and drift.
a181b450: Not every moment needs the strongest version
0adacde3: A system that is maximally strict all the time gets abandoned too. Most of the time you do not need another human involved — you need a two-second interruption to break an automatic reach.
5b689a14: So the useful thing is a range. A gentle reminder for the unconscious grab. A short enforced wait for when you are restless but not committed. And a genuine lock, held by someone else, for the handful of situations where you already know your own promises will not hold.
af08f656: That is exactly how Disconnect's three lock levels are arranged. Soft and Medium work on their own with nobody else involved. Hard lock is the one where a buddy holds the key — and it is the only level where the answer is genuinely out of your hands.
88956bf8: Disconnect blocks the app and hands the key to a friend. All three lock levels, including the one only your buddy can open, are in the free version.
35864817: How to set this up today
d659e13e: Pick one app, not all of them. The one you already know the answer to. Starting with six apps is how people quit in week one.
bdfb68a9: Choose the honest lock level. If you have broken your own limit on this app before, Soft lock will not hold. Use Hard.
2e78eb92: Pick a buddy who will actually say no. Not your most agreeable friend. See how to ask someone.
49dbe1e6: Set the schedule slightly wider than feels comfortable. The edges are where the relapse happens.
2da02533: Leave it alone for two weeks. Adjusting the rule during a craving is just unlocking with extra steps.
429aa790: None of this requires you to become a more disciplined person. It requires the decision to sit somewhere your craving cannot reach.
